title: Hearing before reading
hookLine: the Qur'an is first recited, heard, memorized, and only then read

lines: THE TEXT STARTS IN THE EAR.
cards: Nobody reads the lyrics of a lullaby. A child hears it in the dark, again and again, until one night the child sings it back. The words arrive through the ear.
A mosque classroom on a Saturday morning works the same way: rows of kids, some rocking gently, repeating after a teacher, line by line, until the sound is in them.
Some can recite whole surahs before they can read the script. This camp is about the text itself, and it starts where the text started: in the ear.

teach.b: Muslim scholars connect the word Qur'an to a root meaning to read aloud, to recite: the Qur'an is the recitation.

And tradition says the first word revealed, in a cave outside Mecca, was a command from that same root: iqra'. In Pickthall's translation, Surah al-Alaq opens: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth.
The Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say, could not read or write. So the Qur'an didn't arrive as a book. It arrived as sound, through the angel Jibril, a little at a time, over many years.
The Prophet recited it; the companions heard and memorized it; some wrote it on whatever they had, palm stalks and thin flat stones.
Bukhari reports that every Ramadan, Jibril went over all that had been revealed with him, aloud. Only after the Prophet's death was it gathered into a single written volume.
The word for this reciting is tilawah. Arabic dictionaries give its root the sense of following, one thing after another, the way words follow words.
And scholars point out a second meaning: to follow a text is also to live by it. To this day, the Qur'an is taught mouth to ear, teacher to student, in chains going back generation by generation.
There are rules for how each letter is sounded, called tajwid.
And a report in Abu Dawud says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices. The first listeners met it with their ears, not their eyes.
For the next weeks, this camp walks through the thirtieth part, the last section, full of short surahs.

how: Muslims learn the Qur'an by hearing it recited and repeating after a teacher, often memorizing before reading; many also listen to recordings of reciters.

games.q: you want to learn a short surah. the first listeners in Mecca didn't have printed copies. how did they learn it?
o: by hearing it recited and repeating it
games.why: they heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it and memorized it; some wrote it on palm stalks and stones. it's still taught mouth to ear.

practice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds already around you, the way you'd listen to music in a language you don't know yet: the rise and fall, the long vowels, the pauses.
That's the ear a short surah asks for, al-Fatiha, al-Ikhlas or any of the last ones, heard from a reciter you like, without reading along or reaching for a translation yet.

wordCard.voice: Tilawah. Reciting the Qur'an aloud, from a root meaning to follow: word after word, and then in how you live. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: recitation, from the root t-l-w, to follow.

carryVoice: Your line: hear it first. The sound arrives first, and the meaning follows. Until tomorrow.
